extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters (particularly of New York), legislators, and policymakers debating adoption and design of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and defending the constitutional allocation of taxation powers and the nature of representation in a federal union — arguments about what powers the national government must have and how representation will function. The text offers principles for structuring revenue sources, administration, and representative bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base permanent provisions on permanent causes of expense
rubrics_metrics.description: In framing a government for posterity, permanent provisions (especially revenue allocations) should be calculated on permanent causes of expense, not temporary ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate state needs on permanent, lasting expenses (e.g., civil lists and contingencies — roughly ~200,000 pounds in the essay's example). Do not grant States exclusive revenue sources beyond what their permanent needs require, because doing so can unfairly deprive the Union of necessary resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction in taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrent jurisdiction in taxation (both federal and state authority) is the only admissible substitute for making state authority entirely subordinate with respect to taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent jurisdiction reconciles an indefinite federal power of taxation with an adequate and independent power for the States to provide for their own necessities; it avoids sacrificing Union interests to individual States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite federal power of taxation is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must be vested with a broad, indefinite power of taxation to meet the varied and potentially unlimited exigencies of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting federal taxation to narrow objects (e.g., only imports) would lead to oppression of particular industries, unequal burdens among states and citizens, temptation to overextend specific duties, and inability to meet national obligations (debts, defense, unexpected events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Import duties should go into a common fund and not be the sole national fund
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties on imports should be paid into a common national stock and not be treated as the exclusive national revenue source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on import duties produces inequality among States (importing vs. manufacturing), encourages smuggling, can create monopolies for manufacturers, and may unfairly burden merchants. A common fund avoids concentrating benefit in importing States and permits more equitable distribution of revenue burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes (duties, imposts, excises) must be uniform throughout the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutionally: 'all duties, imposts, and excises shall be UNIFORM throughout the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity is a guard against partiality or oppression by preventing localized, discriminatory tax regimes; it is an explicit constitutional check on abuse of federal taxation authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal taxes subdivided into direct and indirect — national legislature can administer both
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal taxes include direct and indirect taxes; objections to federal administration are weak because the necessary knowledge of local circumstances can be obtained and execution can be delegated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For indirect taxes (duties/excises) the nature of the article often suggests administration; for direct taxes (land, houses) execution relies on local assessors/commissioners. The national legislature can adopt state methods and use local officers to collect taxes, and can avoid conflict by abstaining from objects preoccupied by States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use each State's administrative system within that State
rubrics_metrics.description: The national legislature can adopt and make use of each State's system of laying and collecting taxes within that State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical execution of tax laws (valuations, assessments) requires local officers; federal law should name or prescribe modes for selection and general outlines while leaving local details to local functionaries, thereby avoiding duplication and reducing expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation need not include a member from every occupation to represent interests
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impractical and unnecessary to expect each occupation or class to send members of its own number; merchants, landholders, and learned professions will naturally represent broader groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artisans and manufacturers commonly vote for merchants as their natural patrons; landholders share common interests across wealthy and middling proprietors; learned professions act as impartial arbiters. Thus a representative body composed largely of these groups will, in practice, represent wider interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: National representatives can obtain required local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of local circumstances necessary for taxation (resources, agriculture, commerce, manufactures) can be acquired by national representatives, and detailed local facts can be provided by members from the respective States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration of finances is commonly entrusted to small boards or enlightened statesmen who prepare taxation plans; the national legislature's need is for general principles rather than minute topographical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Census-based apportionment prevents partiality in direct taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions of taxes (e.g., for direct taxes) are to be determined by the numbers of each State as given by a census or enumeration; this rule effectively prevents partiality or favoritism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An objective formula (enumeration) combined with uniformity reduces the risk of arbitrary or oppressive taxation targeted at particular States or groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the power to tax even if requisitions are a fallback
rubrics_metrics.description: Although requisitions on States can be used where federal internal taxation is inconvenient, the Constitution should keep the federal power to tax because it is preferable and strengthens the efficacy of requisitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons: (1) direct exercise of taxation is more effectual if convenient; (2) the existence of taxing power incentivizes States to comply with requisitions, knowing the Union could act without them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double taxation and duplication of revenue officers by coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Fears of duplicate revenue officers and double taxation are overstated; practical solutions include (a) exclusive federal rights where applicable, (b) the Union abstaining from objects preoccupied by States, or (c) using State officers and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using State officers for federal collections saves expense and avoids provoking State governments and the people; mutual abstention and coordination will reduce interference between federal and state revenue systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain power to levy poll taxes for emergencies despite general disapproval
rubrics_metrics.description: Poll taxes are socially unpopular and generally disapproved, but the federal government ought to retain the power to use them in extraordinary emergencies when other resources are scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of the power does not mean it will be used; many States have the same power and rarely employ it. In crises, having the option can be essential for public safety and defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer productive taxation that minimizes burden on the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: A most productive system of finance will also tend to be the least burdensome; policy should aim to use revenue sources (e.g., luxury taxes) that make the wealthy contribute, thereby relieving poorer classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximizing revenue from the capital resource of commercial imposts and taxing luxuries where practicable can reduce reliance on more burdensome taxes on the poor and promote equitable distribution of public burdens.
